messages.subject: RStan memory trivia
parts:
I had sflist the result of 3 parallel runs of my model, and
r4 <- sflist2stanfit(sflist)

r3b was the result of a similar operation.

The process was just over 2G.

save(r3b, r4, sflist, file="r4.rdata")

Surprise #1: the resulting file is 1.8G, which doesn't seem like much
compression.

In another process I

load(file="r4.rdata")

Surprise #2: The new process is just under 4G.

I assume what's going on here is that R tries not to make unnecessary
copies, and so r4 and sflist share most of their memory. But then when
it's written out this association is lost, effectively doubling the
size.

If this theory is right, it seems R could do better.

R 2.15

Ross Boylan

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] RStan memory trivia
parts:
First, thanks for all the thoughtful comments.
Hardly trivia from our perspective!

It's very helpful to get feedback. More below.

On 9/17/13 2:15 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> I had sflist the result of 3 parallel runs of my model, and
> r4 <- sflist2stanfit(sflist)
>
> r3b was the result of a similar operation.
>
> The process was just over 2G.
And that process had both r4 and r3b in memory?
> save(r3b, r4, sflist, file="r4.rdata")

Doesn't this write r3b, r4 AND sflist into the file
r4.data? Is that what you intended?

Why not just write r4?

And I don't see how r3b relates to all this.

> Surprise #1: the resulting file is 1.8G, which doesn't seem like much
> compression.

Surprised that R was so efficient with memory or
surprised it was so wasteful with disk?

It looks like save() just does a binary write. There's
an option for using gzip compression, but I doubt it's
going to help much compared to a binary save with floating
point numbers --- numbers like those from a sampler usually
aren't very predictable from gzip's perspective.

> In another process I
>
> load(file="r4.rdata")
>
> Surprise #2: The new process is just under 4G.
>
> I assume what's going on here is that R tries not to make unnecessary
> copies, and so r4 and sflist share most of their memory. But then when
> it's written out this association is lost, effectively doubling the
> size.
>
> If this theory is right, it seems R could do better.

It'll probably let you garbage collect and bring that back down,
but we don't want to hit dynamic peaks of double the memory we
need if we don't have to.

Scalability's a big deal for us!

Once we understand what you meant to do above, if there's not
an easy fix we should open an RStan issue for this at:

https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/issues

> R 2.15

Thanks for letting us know.

- Bob

On Tue, Sep 17, 2013 at 08:31:28PM -0400, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> First, thanks for all the thoughtful comments.
> Hardly trivia from our perspective!

You'er welcome. First of all, I got confused and things are not as
weird or as bad as my original message implied. In fact, I had which
process had which amount of memory reversed.

Inquiries on the R list and some experiments did confirm that there is
some expansion of memory use in the scenario I outlined (save/load).
In particular, reading in sflist from disk and then constructing r4
from sflist2stanfit uses less memory than reading sflist and r4 from
from disk. The serialization loses the sharing of memory between
sflist and r4. It seemed to be about 300M in this case.

Apparently only environments are shared between objects on
serialization.

> It's very helpful to get feedback. More below.
>

Apparently the theory is right. The R folks are aware of the issue,
but doing better is tricky and it's in the "don't hold your breath"
category.

>
> It'll probably let you garbage collect and bring that back down,
> but we don't want to hit dynamic peaks of double the memory we
> need if we don't have to.
>

>

I don't think this is an issue that can be addressed at the rstan, as
opposed to R, level, unless there are games that could be played with
object representation or even the use of environments.

The operational fix is to avoid saving information that can be derived
from other information.

Ross
